transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Democrats have a nearly two-to-one edge over Republicans when it comes to voter trust on
health care costs, according to a new poll out today, NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin with
details.
The cost of health care is weighing heavily on voters' minds with the midterm elections
just one month away.
That's according to the new poll from KFF, a nonpartisan health research organization.
KFF's Ashley Kurzinger says they polled 1,300 people in mid-September.
What we are seeing is that the Democratic Party has the advantage overall among all
voters on which party voters trust to handle health care, but they also have the advantage
among independent voters, and that's a really important voting block for midterm elections.
Kurzinger says Democrats had a 10-point advantage on health costs in April.
Now that gap has doubled.
22 percent of voters trust Republicans on the issue, compared to 42 percent who trust Democrats.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
High diesel prices are also on many voters' minds.
At a campaign rally in Nebraska last night, President Trump signed an executive order
aimed at lowering diesel fuel costs.
Here's NPR's Frank Ordonez.
President Trump told the audience in the middle of agriculture country that he was signing
the order to help farmers.
The rising cost of fuel has been a significant challenge for Republicans heading into the
midterms.
Prices for diesel used by trucks have been hit particularly hard due to the wars in both
Iran and Ukraine.
The president did not share details, but the order is expected to expand access to diesel,
including so-called red-dye diesel fuel, which is used by the agriculture industry, and not
subject to the same state and federal highway taxes as regular diesel.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
Cornell University has hired former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent
review of the New York school's handling of sexual assault reports.
Yates' previous work investigating abuses in women's professional soccer contributed
to leak-related probes by state attorneys general, including New York AG Letitia James, who a
few days ago was appointed to oversee an investigation into the alleged gang rape of a woman at Cornell
in 2024.
Kenya has announced its first case of Ebola.
Kenya's government has urged people not to panic after it announced its first case of
the disease stemming from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Here's Emmett Livingstone.
Kenya's Health Minister Adendwale said a Kenyan national living in Congo had returned home
infected with the disease.
The patient traveled from Congo to neighboring Uganda by road and from there took a plane
to Nairobi, where he died in hospital.
Adendwale says the authorities are tracing dozens of the patient's contacts, adding that
"all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease."
An Ebola outbreak was declared in eastern Congo in May.
It's since become one of the largest in history, killing more than 4,000 people.
It's NPR.
A U.S. defense official not authorized to speak publicly has confirmed with NPR that
credible threats of Iranian-inspired attacks led the U.S. to move bombers from a British
airbase.
The U.S. withdrew all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers Sunday.
According to the official, the abrupt move had a concern of some kind of attack, including
the possible use of drones.
The state of Texas is investigating whether Haynes and Fruit of the Loom use harmful chemicals
in the manufacture of children's underwear; Texas Attorney General Ken Paxson has not
accused the companies of breaking the law, but today he warned that manufacturers have
increased their use of synthetic fabrics that can be harmful to children; the Republicans
running against Democrat James Tallarico for the U.S. Senate.
A number of polls suggest Paxson is trailing his rival ahead of the midterms in less than
a month.
The Nobel Prize in Physics has gone to a researcher who led an effort to build a giant particle
detector in Antarctica, and Pierre-Steph Bromfield has more on what it found.
Francis Hallson has spent his career chasing ghostly particles known as neutrinos.
Neutrinos rarely interact with regular matter, but when they do, they create a tiny flash
of light.
Hallson, at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, developed a plan to place detectors in a cubic
kilometer of ice in Antarctica.
At the time, it seemed like a longshot.
The detector, called Ice Cube, won the prize for finding high-energy neutrinos from deep
space.
Jeff Bromfield, NPR News.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News, in Washington.
